Chickens are nice but not as easy to play with as cats or dogs, not many people do fun things with their chickens. Here's a thread that might help. If you have multiple chickens, grape football sounds entertaining.
Easy and simple: Take a couple breasts, rub a little avacado oil on (or olive oil if avacado isn't available), good sprinkle of garlic salt, and broil it for ~10 minutes per side.
I prefer to grill. A BIG tip is to season it with spices instead of sauces.

Make your own chicken broth.

All you need is:

  • one chicken breast, skinless but with the bone in.

  • some vegetables. whatever you have on hand but it's always a good idea to include your basic aromatics: onion, celery and carrot.

Fill a large stockpot with water, add your chicken breast and vegetables; bring to a boil and then lower the heat and let it simmer for about an hour. The veggies will turn to mush afterwards so scoop those out. Remove the chicken, strip it up and use it for anything from chicken salad to chicken soup or a casserole and there you have it: the base for tons of soups and other recipes. Try freezing it in ice cube trays. Also, you can use vegetable scraps from other meals you've prepared; just keep the skins and cuttings in the refrigerator until stock day!

Curry! Just chicken, a bunch of left over vegetables, a can of tomatoes, coconut milk, and spices (pepper, cumin, cinnamon, a good masala powder)... . There are so many different curry recipes, but if you have those ingredients on hand, you should be able to make something!

Is it possible for an antenna telly to pick up radio/microwaves from the past? For instance, could I hear the D-Day broadcast on a radio, or watch the first Superbowl on an antenna TV by picking up radio waves? A small portion of the static on a telly comes from the big bang, so would it be possible to somehow view former broadcasts from these signals? If not, why? I'm sorry if this is a stupid question. I know nothing about wave transmission and such.

Thanks!
Would it be possible to view/listen to TV/radio broadcasts from the past that are picked up by an antenna? Why or why not?
Radio waves travel with the speed of light, the furthest possible to hear into the future is radio waves bounced by moon, it's about 2 seconds delayed and needs special equipment.

The reason people say that the static on your screen is Big Bang microwave radiation is because the radiation from the Big Bang permeates the entire universe. It's known as the Cosmic Microwave Background.

As /u/Stavon pointed out, radio waves reflected by the moon, or potentially other astronomical objects, can be picked up. For objects further than the moon from Earth, the likelihood of a precise, strong enough reflection back towards a receiver is unlikely.

But radio waves do keep travelling beyond the Solar System. As radio waves are, basically, a form of light, they travel at light speed. Here's a thought experiment. Imagine you had a spaceship, capable of faster-than-light travel. One day, you decide to transmit a message toward Jupiter, before hopping into your spaceship and travelling there yourself.

Let's assume that you can precisely target these radio waves, and that your ship is also capable of staying in orbit near to the planet.

The radio wave's flight time there would be around 33 minutes. For the sake of the thought experiment, we'll say you can reach Jupiter in 25 minutes. So you do. And you set up a little receiving station in orbit around the gas giant. Sure enough, 8 minutes after you arrive near Jupiter, the message you transmitted from Earth arrives on your receiving station.

As radio waves travel at light speed, they can travel astonishing distances from Earth and maintain some degree of clarity in a relatively short time. Imagine we have a colony ship 1 light year away headed towards a nearby star. If they tune into the Earth broadcasts, they'll find themselves watching ones that happened a year ago, because it took the radio wave 1 year to travel the distance between Earth and the colony ship.

The further away you travel from Earth, the older the radio waves you can pick up with your antenna. You might be inclined to think that, since we've been transmitting for at least a century, you could travel far enough and listen to Hitler giving one of his nationalistic rallies. Unfortunately, this isn't the case, as after around 4 light years (that's a distance, not a time period), the radio waves become so weak that they become indistinguishable from the cosmic microwave background.

So, in summary, yes! You can listen to past radio broadcasts on Earth if they're reflected off of a nearby object, or you can travel stupidly large distances to hear older ones, up to around 4 years in age!
